The Yeoville Dinner Club

By: Zikhona Tshona | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we dine with the world, from right here in Johannesburg

Unique Selling Point:
A dinner club of strangers at the heart of Joburg

Summary:
When people think of Yeoville, they think dilapidated buildings, hustle and bustle, sometimes crime, just chaos. It's hard to imagine the the area was once the hub of South Africa's arts and music; also known for being vibrant and culturally diverse. Now, tt's an utter mess with neglected infrastructure and dirty streets

In the middle of all that chaos is a dinner club that has hosted people from the world over. Guests, mostly tourists, sit along long tables and share a meal with strangers from different  parts of the world while Chef Sandile Sanza serves dishes and drinks from countries on the continent. Each dish has a story and Sanza shares his wealth of knowledge not only of South Africa, but of the continent. It's about people coming together to experience Africa through food, music and art.

Sanza Sandile founded the Dinner Club because he once lived there and wanted to revive or contribute to what it was once known for. He's cooked for some well known celebrities both locally and internationally. He has just returned from a US tour of sharing African cuisines.

Script:


(Claire) Yeoville: an area once known for its effortless cool. In the 90s, this was the place to be for entertainment and nightlife.

(Fred) So, this is Rockey Street. At the beginning of Rockey Street there are places such as Time Square. So, in that precinct you would get La Copa restaurant. And if you are interested in chicken curry or Durban curry, there was Cherros.

(Claire) Award-winning author Fred Khumalo knew Yeoville in its heyday when living there made it possible to imagine a new South Africa.

(Fred) The Group Areas Act was repealed in 1986. So, Yeoville and Hillbrow started opening up even back then. But after 1994, things just happened so fast, so quickly. So, with people moving from all over, people like me moving from Durban, others moving from different parts of the country and the world, finding this place. And it immediately became a microcosm of what South Africa, the future South Africa could be like.

(Claire) As time passed, Yeoville became better known for its urban decay. Many residents left and never looked back.

(Claire) When I first came to Yeoville in the 90s, it was a magical, vibrant place. Looking around now, it's hard to imagine it the way it once was. But there's one man that's fighting hard to preserve this community and that Yeoville spirit.

(Claire) That man is Sandile Tshabalala, better known as Sanza. A foodie and storyteller still rooted in this area. He has made it his mission not to leave Yeoville, but instead to share its story.

(Sanza) Hello, Claire. How are you? Welcome to Yeoville. Come upstairs now.

(Claire) I'm coming, I’m coming.

(Claire) What are your earliest memories of Yeoville?

(Sanza) Sure. I used to play in the Carlton Centre, and I lived in Hillbrow and I was studying that side of town. And we had to always tuck in your T-shirt or tie up your jeans so, you know, when you're coming to Yeoville. Because Yeoville was very stylish. Peggy-Sue Khumalo used to be Miss South Africa, but she was working at a wine bar called La Copa in Time Square. And everybody wanted to be served by her because she's Miss South Africa. There was a guy called Fikile Magadlela, some uncle that I liked, and then he was a poet and a painter.
The black eccentrics were in Yeoville, teaching us how to eat, how to greet, how to dress and how to play music, how to listen to music.

(Claire) To this day, this is the neighborhood where Africa meets in music, food and shared life. Sanza is using food to bring strangers together through his Yeoville Dinner Club. It's no traditional restaurant, but a social dining experience hosted by Sanza himself. Guests gather around a single table to share African food and stories.

(Sanza) I'm just using, you know, my dinner club or my stories just to remind us how far we've come and everything I learned here in Yeoville; how to eat, how to cook. Thirty years later, I'm still learning and trying to recreate those memories.

(Claire) Once a popular radio personality, Sanza ditched his job in the 90s to follow his true passion – food.

(Sanza) I'd been cooking since food was R5. My supper club was R5 a head at a house in Berea. I’m obsessed with tofu and all the vegetables that you'd find in the Chinese market. And I'd come back, and I had a wok – which was a strange pot – and a wok could do everything. So, I carry a wok and I’ve got tofu, and I’ve got this, and I go to a health shop and can buy some nuts.
.
(Claire) And it's here at the Yeoville Market, with all its African delicacies, that he has the most fun.

(Sanza) And then you get advice. When you buy something, people want… What do you want to? How do you want to cook? You know, the aunties are always there to share their culture. I don't come in knowing too much. You know what I'm trying to say? Come and ask and learn, and then… Then you get home, then you take it further.

(Sanza) I've learned to buy ingredients. I do cooking classes informally in Yeoville. Yeoville has always been progressive. It's a space to learn, to grow. People are sophisticated here.

(Claire) Thank you so much.

(Claire) Walking around with Sanza feels like I'm walking around with encyclopedic knowledge of African cuisine and the history of Yeoville. The more he talks, the more wealth comes out. Wow, wow, wow!

(Sanza) You know, the cultural practitioners somehow…

(Claire) In 2010, during the Football World Cup in South Africa, Sanza decided to take his food to the streets.

(Sanza) I was grilling fish in the streets. I was making falafels. I was making some kind of puthu with egusi. And I was, like, taking Pan-African dishes, making them strictly vegan without adding the other shrimps and other things. Because, you know, people are sensitive in different ways. And also, I'm all-encompassing. You know, the way I love people I can, like, replace… I can lick a stone and put it in the pot instead of salt.

(Claire) And the world responded. He met internationally renowned celebrity chef Anthony Bourdain, best known for documenting the cultures and cuisines of less-travelled places.

(Sanza) Some girl wrote an article about the World Cup. Anthony Bourdain read about it. The guy smuggling dishes, he's not from all of these countries. But he's cooking the dishes from all those countries. And then, Bourdain calls me two weeks later. They were here with like a 20-member crew shooting me, wanting to hear the stories of Yeoville.

(Claire) It sparked a new dream to bring people to his beloved neighbourhood and change the perception that Yeoville is a no-go zone.

(Sanza) Now, this dish was inspired by India. And now, when I put tomato and basil, it makes me think of Italy when you make pomodoro. It's going to be a crazy salad! People won't know what the devil is in there!

(Sanza) My concept is called The Gastronomic Smuggler. I feel like I'm always smuggling flavours, smuggling stories, you know? And I go to the Yeoville Market. The market was called the Congolese Market when it started.

(Sanza) I just love this country, guys. And I love this city, and I love this town called Yoeville. Yeoville’s got a different heart. I made an Egyptian recipe kind of chicken. It's not a jollof, but it's inspired by a jollof rice inspired by Diri Djon Djon. Please enjoy. Please enjoy.

(Claire) The Yeoville Dinner Club, where word of mouth brings strangers together.

(Vox Pop 1) I think what surprised me is when you walk in, you won't expect what you find. And it's like you’re outside, but when you're walking, you find a home, find peace, comfort, calmness, amazingness. So, I think that's what surprised me. Because, as you’re walking and coming in, you're like not sure, not sure. Then walk into heaven. It's like, that's how it felt.

(Vox Pop 2) Everything was, like, slightly different flavours. But everything goes together super-well. And I like that it's from like different influences from different parts of Africa. So, you kind of get a little taste of like Ghana, a little bit of South Africa. Very cool.

(Claire) Sanza has turned his passion for food and stories into a culinary and cultural institution.

(Claire) He’s even taking his club on tour, having just recently returned from a trip to the United States of America.

(Sanza) It blew up. I got to Atlanta Airport, I put my hashtag Yeoville Dinner Club... All my dinners – about 19 of them I did in the US – half the people had been to my actual physical space here in Yeoville Dinner Club. And they'd seen that I'm in the US. They would take flights and trains and buses to be where it was near to them, and then all the time when I opened up my dinner club, I said, “Who's been to Yeoville?” Half the table raised their hand, and half have been bought by the friends we've seen.

(Claire) Like many others, Khumalo has moved out of Yeoville. But he says Sanza’s dinner club is exactly what the suburb and its legacy are all about.

(Fred) Sanza was here when I got here in 1995. And he's always been involved in the culinary space, cooking and hosting people. So, I'm saying this man has got staying power. And he still attracts a lot of clientele, obviously, because of where the place is located. It's mainly tourists from overseas who come here, and they come consistently.

(Sanza) You know, in Yeoville again, I just thought all these people around here, they must have grown up somewhere and they had a granny who made something. So, we are all here for a reason. We were all eating something. So, I respect all people's foods, and I thought I'd go towards those kinds of things. I started also remembering my upbringing. How do you make people feel at home? This is the New York of Africa. So, when you come with ideas, if you are naughty from Bujumbura in Johannesburg, you can even be better.

(Claire) And here, at this table, Yeoville itself is reflected: bold, blended and inviting you back for more.
